transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-02
Start time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Heller (Redwood SE), Sofia Ramirez (Verdant CTO), Evan Cole (Verdant Platform Eng), Priya Nair (Verdant Head Security)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping to prove private connectivity, no internet egress, region-locking, and benchmark expected latency/throughput for a 7b model inference (we discussed model variants + batching + cost tradeoffs). Agreed to run a two-hour benchmark window, Redwood to share PrivateLink CFN, customer to share traffic profile and compliance checklist.

Topics:
- VPC Peering vs PrivateLink (security, egress behavior)
- Regions and residency (us-east-1 primary, eu-west-1 fallback)
- Egress constraints (deny internet, allow S3 via VPC endpoints?)
- Benchmark plan: p95 latency, tokens/sec, concurrency, memory footprint
- Success criteria and timelines for POC

Notes / Shared artifacts: deck: https://drive.google.com/verdant-poc-deck (note: access pending), benchmark sheet: https://sheets.example.com/verdant-bench-ctrl, infra snippets: private-link-cfn.yaml (attached in chat).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: alright uh hey everyone thanks for carving out time today, this is Lena from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. we also have Marcus on the call who's going to lead the technical bits. quick intros?
[00:08] Sofia Ramirez: hi lena, sofia here, CTO at verdant, thanks. evan and priya with me. we want to lock down how a poc would look for private networking + data residency.
[00:15] Marcus Heller: hey team, marcus, redwood SE. i'll focus on benchmarks and networking.
[00:20] Evan Cole: evan, platform eng. we own vpc and infra.
[00:23] Priya Nair: priya, security. i'll be focused on the compliance side and egress policy.
[00:26] Lena Park: awesome. high-level goal — you told us earlier you need zero internet egress for model calls and that data must stay in us-east-1 unless failover. is that still accurate?
[00:36] Sofia Ramirez: yep that's the big one. also we need to understand latency impacts and cost tradeoffs if we use privatelink vs peering. and we want a repeatable benchmark so legal/ops can sign off.
[00:46] Marcus Heller: perfect. quick clarifying q: what model size are you planning to run in the POC— 7b, 13b? that affects GPU selection and KV cache.
[00:54] Evan Cole: we're targeting a quantized 7b to start. production might use 13b later but we want baseline perf for 7b. expected RPS is around 80 requests per second at peak, average payload 600 tokens per request, concurrency about 40 active streams.
[01:09] Marcus Heller: great, that's helpful. for 7b with those numbers we're thinking 2xA10 nodes for the bench with batching and kv cache; p95 target latency we'd aim for <= 220ms for small prompts and <= 700ms for conversational turn lengths (600 tokens is… that increases decoding time). the bench will measure p50/p90/p95 and tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and memory footprint.
[01:35] Priya Nair: question — we cannot have calls to the public internet for inference traffic. does privatelink fully prevent egress? we need to be explicit.
[01:43] Marcus Heller: good question. PrivateLink keeps traffic within aws network and the service endpoint— it avoids NAT gateway egress to the internet. with PrivateLink the traffic goes over the AWS private network to Redwood's NLB in the region. with VPC peering, traffic is routed to the peered vpc ip space, so both can avoid internet egress, but peering requires more routing table changes and cross-account peering if that's your setup. both can be configured with no internet egress, but you need to ensure no route out via a nat gateway and block egress via SG/NACL.
[02:15] Evan Cole: ok, but what about S3 egress — we sometimes need to pull configs/artifacts. can that be allowed without opening internet?
[02:22] Lena Park: yes, you can allow S3 via VPC endpoint (gateway endpoint) or restrict to specific buckets using VPC endpoint policies. we usually recommend explicit allow for the buckets used in the POC and block all other egress.
[02:33] Priya Nair: what about KMS usage— keys must be customer-managed and never leave region. can redwood integrate with our KMS?
[02:40] Marcus Heller: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for Hosted with PrivateLink we can integrate with customer KMS via cross-account key policies and ensure logs show envelope metadata. there may be some differences in Private vs Hosted but for the POC we can use a customer-managed CMK in us-east-1. we'll share the exact policy snippet.
[03:02] Sofia Ramirez: okay good. timeline wise— we want bench results next week ideally, is that realistic?
[03:08] Marcus Heller: yes if we get sample traffic and credentials today or tomorrow we can schedule a 2-hour bench window mid next week. we'll need Evan to open a test VPC endpoint or peering and provide ephemeral IAM creds for the test.
[03:20] Evan Cole: i can provision a privatelink endpoint in our account and give you the endpoint service name and an IAM role for the test. i need the exact CloudFormation snippet or runbook.
[03:30] Lena Park: we'll send CFN and a runbook. i will also share a short doc comparing peering vs privatelink pros/cons for security and ops.
[03:38] Priya Nair: one more: audit logs and retention — we need to capture every request metadata and keep it for 180 days. is that supported?
[03:45] Marcus Heller: yes, Redwood Console has per-request tracing and you can export logs to your S3 via our retention pipeline. for PrivateLink we can push audit logs into your account with a service role; retention and lifecycle policies are in your bucket. we'll confirm retention and encryption in the runbook.
[04:00] Sofia Ramirez: we also need a clear success criteria for legal: no internet egress, p95 latency under 1s for 600-token requests, and cost estimate within 3x our current inference infra cost.
[04:12] Lena Park: ok we'll formalize success criteria— sounds like three bullets: network+residency pass (no egress & us-east-1), perf pass (p95 <= 1s for target workload), cost estimate within 3x. any other must-have?
[04:25] Priya Nair: encryption in transit and at rest, SSO integration (SAML), SOC2 evidence—those are must-haves but more for later sign-off. for POC we mainly need encryption confirmed and audit logs working.
[04:37] Marcus Heller: noted. we'll attach SOC2 summary and SAML notes but won't block the bench on full SAML setup.
[04:45] Evan Cole: about region lock — we'd like primary in us-east-1 but a manual failover to eu-west-1 if needed. do you support region routing?
[04:53] Marcus Heller: yes, our smart routing can pin to a region and we can configure manual or canary failover to eu-west-1. for the POC we can keep everything in us-east-1. if you want a failover test, we can schedule additional validation.
[05:05] Sofia Ramirez: cool. now on benchmarks— please talk through the exact tests you'll run.
[05:09] Marcus Heller: sure. plan A: load test at the expected peak 80 RPS with a 40 concurrent window. We'll run three phases: ramp (10 minutes), steady-state (60 minutes) and soak (50 minutes) but for the two-hour window we'll do ramp (10m), 100% steady (70m), short spike tests (40m). measurements: p50/p90/p95/p99, start-to-first-token latency, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization, mem usage, and network bytes. We'll also test with and without batching and with prefix/KV cache warmed.
[05:42] Evan Cole: can we get a cost estimate for the bench? we have budget constraints; we want to make sure a two-hour run won't surprise finance.
[05:48] Lena Park: absolutely — we'll provide a bench cost estimate. typically the bench nodes for a 7b quantized model are moderate, estimate ~$300-700 for a 2-hour run depending on GPU type; we'll refine after selecting instance types.
[06:02] Priya Nair: also we need to ensure egress is provable — like can you show packet traces or flow logs that show no internet NAT?
[06:09] Marcus Heller: yes we can capture VPC Flow Logs and our side will capture service-side access logs; we'll provide a short checklist for what to look for (no 0.0.0.0/0 route, no NAT gateway).
[06:20] [slight crosstalk] Sofia Ramirez: sounds good— you mentioned protec… protec— sorry— pricing. is cost-per-inference metrics baked into the console?
[06:28] Lena Park: yes, Console provides token-level cost estimates and per-route breakdowns. for the POC we'll provide a simple sheet that maps measured tokens/sec and average token length to cost per 1k tokens.
[06:36] Evan Cole: ok, technical nit: we use strict egress rules that require endpoints to be in the same AZ where possible; does PrivateLink require cross-AZ traffic?
[06:44] Marcus Heller: PrivateLink endpoints are regional and will do cross-AZ when the NLB is regional. we can advise on AZ placement and recommend replicating endpoints for production to avoid cross-AZ data transfer charges, but for the POC one endpoint in us-east-1 should be fine.
[06:59] Sofia Ramirez: what about SNI and TLS termination— we need TLS end-to-end, no termination in an external network.
[07:05] Marcus Heller: TLS is end-to-end between client and Redwood service. we can use mutual TLS if you want extra assurances— though PrivateLink already keeps traffic on the AWS backbone, mTLS gives application-level auth.
[07:18] Priya Nair: good. okay practical steps— what do you need from us to start?
[07:22] Lena Park: list of items: 1) sample payloads and a synthetic traffic profile (RPS/concurrency distribution), 2) an infra contact to create the PrivateLink endpoint or accept peering, 3) example S3 buckets and KMS key ARNs if you want us to access artifacts, 4) acceptance criteria confirmation.
[07:35] Evan Cole: will do. i'll send payload samples and ian, our infra lead, will create the endpoint.
[07:40] Sofia Ramirez: is there any reason to choose peering instead of Privatelink in our case? we run multiple accounts and prefer least ops overhead.
[07:48] Marcus Heller: peering can be simpler if both accounts are tightly controlled and you want full VPC-level access, but it can complicate routing and increase blast radius. PrivateLink is usually preferred for cross-account because it limits exposure and is easier to manage with endpoint policies. given your security posture, PrivateLink sounds like the default recommendation.
[08:06] Priya Nair: one more point — we do strict data residency for logs too. can you keep logs in our S3 and not replicate them out of region?
[08:13] Lena Park: yes, we can write logs to your S3 in us-east-1 and set lifecycle to 180 days; we won't replicate unless you opt in.
[08:20] [small pause] 
[08:25] Marcus Heller: i'll outline the bench steps in the runbook: endpoint creation, sample payload upload, warm cache, run phases, collect metrics, provide artifacts (grafana, perf traces, flow logs).
[08:34] Evan Cole: what about authentication — do you support IAM-based auth over PrivateLink?
[08:39] Marcus Heller: yes, we support signed requests (AWS SigV4) and token-based auth. for PrivateLink we'll use IAM role + signed requests and optionally mutual TLS for app-level auth.
[08:50] Sofia Ramirez: ok sounds like we have alignment. can you summarize the success criteria one more time so i can paste it into the procurement ticket?
[08:56] Lena Park: sure — three success criteria: (1) Network/residency: all inference traffic stays within AWS private network, no internet egress, data and logs remain in us-east-1 unless manual failover. (2) Performance: p95 latency <= 1s for the 600-token workload at target concurrency, tokens/sec consistent with 80 RPS. (3) Cost: bench-based estimate for production operations within 3x of your current infra run rate. also a soft requirement: audit logs captured and encrypted with your CMK and retained 180 days.
[09:24] Priya Nair: that's perfect.
[09:27] Lena Park: great. i'll send the CFN and peering vs privatelink doc after the call, marcus will send the runbook and bench plan.
[09:35] Marcus Heller: i'll also attach the kernel/quantization notes showing expected memory footprint for the 7b model.
[09:42] Evan Cole: timeline check — we'll aim to have endpoints + payloads by monday 2026-10-05 so we can bench mid next week. does that work?
[09:50] Lena Park: yes that's ideal. we'll tentatively reserve a bench window wednesday 2026-10-14, pending your confirmation.
[09:57] Sofia Ramirez: note — legal wants a simple one-week trial contract. can you share a short form agreement and a SOC2 table?
[10:05] Lena Park: yes we'll send a short trial agreement and the SOC2 summary.
[10:10] [brief overlap] Priya Nair: also please include the SAML/OAuth notes for console access for our auditors.
[10:16] Marcus Heller: will do.
[10:18] Lena Park: any other open questions?
[10:20] Sofia Ramirez: none from me. thanks, this was helpful.
[10:23] Evan Cole: all good.
[10:24] Priya Nair: good.
[10:26] Lena Park: ok we'll send notes and next steps — thanks everyone.
[10:30] [meeting ends] 

Post-call recap (auto-summary style):
- Redwood to provide PrivateLink CFN, peering vs PrivateLink doc, runbook, benchmark plan, SOC2 summary, and short trial agreement.
- Verdant to provide payload samples, create PrivateLink endpoint or peering, provide KMS ARNs and S3 buckets, and confirm acceptance criteria.
- Bench target: 2-hour run to measure p95 latency, tokens/sec, mem/GPU usage. Success = no internet egress + p95 <= 1s + cost <= 3x current infra.

Action items (reiterated):
- Lena: send docs and trial agreement (due 2026-10-06)
- Marcus: bench plan + runbook + quant notes (due 2026-10-09)
